docs.text: I've been immersed in D&D for over two decades - ever since I stumbled upon my father's vintage collection – back when Elves and Dwarves were classes, not races! With this, I bring a deep understanding of the game's evolution to the table. I run my games on FoundryVTT, a platform that's both powerful and free for players. While I'm comfortable with theater of the mind, I also utilize maps for those who crave a more visual and tactical experience. My passion lies in crafting RP games with dynamic combat. Think engaging roleplay with a focus on a blooming narrative, but don't worry about the lack of crunchy combat. Whether you're a seasoned adventurer or a wide-eyed newcomer, I'm excited to welcome you to my table. I love fostering a fun and inclusive environment where everyone feels comfortable contributing to the story.

docs.text: Prestige Classes Prestige classes offer specialized, powerful progression paths that characters can choose to pursue once they meet specific requirements. Class Name Description Prerequisites Source Sellsword Blades-for-hire and mercenaries who have gathered a raft of tricks to give them an edge when life and death are on the line. Have completed at least one contract for mercenary work Mage Hand Press Scoundrel Individuals deep in the criminal underworld, adept at keeping secrets, thieves' cant, and watching their backs. Have joined a criminal organization Mage Hand Press Relic Keeper Wielders of mysterious, sentient weapons that are linked to their soul and grow in might alongside them. None Mage Hand Press Pugilist Bare-knuckle brawlers who have mastered an unarmed killer edge through prize fighting or hand-to-hand bouts. None Mage Hand Press Priest Ordained ministers focused on a quieter life with the church, conducting services, and performing community rituals. Must be ordained by some faith Mage Hand Press Hedge Wizard Self-taught magic users who discovered arcana through experimentation and are exceptionally well-versed in cantrips. Spellcasting or Pact Magic feature Mage Hand Press Expert Diligent researchers who have mastered new crafts, honed specific skills, and improved their book smarts. None Mage Hand Press Dragon Acolyte Followers of ancient wyrms who learn to emulate their masters and capture a semblance of draconic might. Allied with a dragon or an aspect of the dragon god Mage Hand Press Cultist Indoctrinated members of secret societies dedicated to terrible, extradimensional beings. Have joined a cult or gained one or more Indefinite Madness traits Mage Hand Press Courier Traders, smugglers, and messengers with a second sense for navigation and traveling quickly. None Mage Hand Press

docs.text: Companions: Sidekicks, Cohorts, and Hirelings While adventurers are the primary heroes of the story, they are occasionally joined by NPC companions who grow and level alongside them. Companion Types Cohorts: Unique companions tied to the Captain class and the Leadership feat. These companions benefit directly from the Captain's stats. Hirelings: Retainers ranging from simple commoners to trained combatants. They generally require payment for their ongoing services. Sidekicks: NPCs recruited along the party's journey, ranging from an awakened cat to a prisoner kobold. Experience and Challenge Rating Bringing companions into battle adjusts the overall Challenge Rating (CR) of the encounter, but they do not penalize the party's experience gain. Instead, they earn an equal share of the experience point pool. For example, if experience is split three ways between the player characters, a sidekick or cohort will also earn that exact same value. Companion Classes When a companion joins the party, they can be assigned one of the following classes to govern their progression. Class Name Description Prerequisites Source Warrior A companion that grows in martial prowess as it fights alongside you, such as a soldier, town guard, or battle-trained beast. None Core Rules Undead A silent, obedient undead thrall, such as a zombie, ghoul, or revenant, raised through necromancy. Any Undead Valda's Spire of Secrets Templar A daring knight sworn to virtue and station, knowing no fear in their heart and no equal in battle. Any Humanoid Valda's Spire of Secrets Steed A faithful mount that serves as a reliable, long-term adventuring companion. None Kibbles' Compendium Spellcaster A companion with magic in their veins, such as a hedge wizard, priest, soothsayer, or magical performer. Must have at least one language in its stat block that it can speak. Core Rules Scoundrel A stealthy and subversive companion who is as adept an assassin as they are a burglar or thief. Any Humanoid Valda's Spire of Secrets Mage A brilliant and studious spellcaster well-versed in the study of all things arcane. Any Humanoid Valda's Spire of Secrets Hunter A naturally skilled tracker and outlander comfortable in the depths of the woods. Any Humanoid Valda's Spire of Secrets Expert A master of tasks and knowledge who favors cunning over brawn. Must have at least one language in its stat block that it can speak. Core Rules Doggo A unique sidekick class to represent only the bestest of traveling companions. Typically limited to doggos, or creatures considered a doggo by their companions. KCLL

Ability Score Choices You may choose one of the following methods to generate your six ability scores. Generation Method Details Min-Max Array 18, 14, 12, 8, 8, 8 Specialist Array 17, 15, 13, 12, 10, 8 Generalist Array 15, 14, 14, 14, 12, 12 Point Buy 27 points to spend (Minimum score 8, Maximum score 17 before species bonuses). Old School Roll Roll 4d6, drop the lowest die. Do this six times. Then assign the scores to your. !!! info "DM's Thoughts: Rolling vs. Reliability" I include the 'Old School Roll' with a swap option because discovering your character's strengths through the dice, rather than engineering them, can lead to highly memorable roleplay. However, Point Buy or an Array are highly recommended if you prefer a tightly balanced build. Starting Gear & Money When creating a character, you must decide how you acquired your starting equipment. Choose one of the following paths: Standard Issue: Take the starting equipment packages granted by your class and background. Note* you may sell items for 50% the value from this to gain some additional starter gold. Starting Wealth: Forgo the equipment packages entirely and roll for starting gold based on your class table in the Player's Handbook (Chapter 5). You must purchase all weapons, armor, and packs from this pool. Bonus Trinket: Regardless of your choice above, every character begins with one item rolled randomly from the Gothic Trinkets table. This changes when you start at a level higher than 4th. 5th-8th level = 500gp plus 1d10x25gp & Normal Starting Equipment 9th-12th level = 5000gp plus 1d10x250gp, two uncommon items, & Normal Starting Equipment 13th-16th level =12000gp plus 1d10x250gp, two uncommon items, one rare item, & Normal Starting Equipment 17th-20th level = 20,000gp plus 1d10×250gp, three uncommon magic items, two rare items, one very rare item, normal starting equipment !!! info "DM's Thoughts: The Value of Scarcity" I lean heavily into the resource management aspect of the game. Choosing to roll for starting wealth is a gamble—you might afford premium armor, or you might start with just a dagger and a backpack. Scarcity drives early-game motivation, making your first major treasure haul feel incredible.

You must purchase all weapons, armor, and packs from this pool. Bonus Trinket: Regardless of your choice above, every character begins with one item rolled randomly from the Gothic Trinkets table. This changes when you start at a level higher than 4th. 5th-8th level = 500gp plus 1d10x25gp & Normal Starting Equipment 9th-12th level = 5000gp plus 1d10x250gp, two uncommon items, & Normal Starting Equipment 13th-16th level =12000gp plus 1d10x250gp, two uncommon items, one rare item, & Normal Starting Equipment 17th-20th level = 20,000gp plus 1d10×250gp, three uncommon magic items, two rare items, one very rare item, normal starting equipment !!! info "DM's Thoughts: The Value of Scarcity" I lean heavily into the resource management aspect of the game. Choosing to roll for starting wealth is a gamble—you might afford premium armor, or you might start with just a dagger and a backpack. Scarcity drives early-game motivation, making your first major treasure haul feel incredible.

docs.text: Combat Modifications We use a few variant rules to speed up encounters and reward tactical positioning. Actions in Combat There are some default actions that almost everyone can do. Here is a list with decriptions. Standard Action Casting a spell: Characters with the spellcasting feature can choose to cast a spell. Attack (melee, unarmed, or ranged): Anyone can choose to attack on their turn, martial classes often get to take multiple swings when they choose to attack. Use a consumable: Most consumables have additional effects when used with an action, but can also be used as a bonus action. Activate a Magic Item: Unless otherwise stated, magic items take an action to activate. Dodge: Take a defensive stance, causing enemies to attack with disadvantage and allows player to roll dexterity saves with advantage Dash: Allows you to move your entire speed an additional time this round Disengage: Allows you to move your entire speed without provoking an attack of opportunity Bonus Action Use a class feature: Use a consumable: Interaction Open a container or Door: Unsheath a weapon: Movement Shift: A creature may choose to move shift 5-feet without provoking attacks of opportunity. This consumes all the movement on the turn and does not count as normal movement. Run: If a creature forgo's it's standard and bonus action for the round, they move 4 times their movement speed in a straight line. They do however lose their dexterity bonus for any attacks of opportunity attacks that are provided during this action. Move: Each creature may move up to it's speed per turn, using what ever appropriate movement type at the time. Reaction Attack of Opportunity: When a creature leaves an area threatened by another, it provokes an attack of opportunity which allows a single attack with a melee or armed attack. Potions as a Bonus Action Drinking a potion yourself: You may use a Standard Action to gain the full amount from a potion, or a bonus action to roll for HP. Administering a potion to an ally: Requires a Standard Action. Modified Flanking Instead of granting advantage (which often invalidates class features and spells), flanking grants a +2 bonus to melee attack rolls against the flanked creature. Find Familiar When you Cast a Spell with a range of touch, or cast a cantrip, your familiar can deliver the spell as if it had cast the spell. Your familiar must be within 100 feet of you, and it must use its Reaction to deliver the spell when you cast it. If the spell requires an Attack roll, you use your Attack modifier for the roll. Two-weapon Fighting and the Nick Mastery When taking the attack action, you may take a single free attack with a different weapon that you're holding in the other hand instead of requiring a bonus action. All other two-weapon fighting rules apply. For example, must be light weapons without the two-weapon fighting feat, and the offhand doesn't apply the modifier to damage. Unarmed strikes count for monks, unarmed fighting style fighters, puglists, and dance bards, and they may make one extra off-hand attack without spending a bonus action. Flurry of blows will still take a bonus action + a ki point to increase the number of bonus attacks from 1 to two. Nick Weapon Mastery - Mastery with a weapon that has the Nick Property will give you one additional attack as part of the Attack action with that weapon Example: A 5th fighter wielding two scimitars(nick) who takes the Attack action would strike four times. Twice from the Extra Attack feature, once from wielding a light weapon in their off-hand, and once from the Nick Property weapon mastery. Leaving the bonus action for something else, such as a scimitar of speed's bonus action attack, a potion, or a class feature.
